claim: Retinal neurons prefer flashing spots of light.
source: Retinal neurons prefer flashing spots of light, primary visual cortical (V1) neurons prefer moving bars, and those in higher cortical areas favor complex features like moving textures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about visual neuron preferences in the abstract.

claim: Primary visual cortical (V1) neurons prefer moving bars.
source: Retinal neurons prefer flashing spots of light, primary visual cortical (V1) neurons prefer moving bars, and those in higher cortical areas favor complex features like moving textures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about V1 neuron preferences in the abstract.

claim: Neurons in higher cortical areas favor complex features like moving textures.
source: Retinal neurons prefer flashing spots of light, primary visual cortical (V1) neurons prefer moving bars, and those in higher cortical areas favor complex features like moving textures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about higher cortical area neuron preferences in the abstract.

claim: V1 simple cell tuning can be accounted for by a basic model implementing temporal prediction.
source: Previously, we showed that V1 simple cell tuning can be accounted for by a basic model implementing temporal prediction – representing features that predict future sensory input from past input (Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Hierarchical application of temporal prediction can capture how tuning properties change across at least two levels of the visual system.
source: Here, we show that hierarchical application of temporal prediction can capture how tuning properties change across at least two levels of the visual system.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The brain does not efficiently represent all incoming information; instead, it selectively represents sensory inputs that help in predicting the future.
source: This suggests that the brain does not efficiently represent all incoming information; instead, it selectively represents sensory inputs that help in predicting the future.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model's success in capturing visual system properties.

claim: When applied hierarchically, temporal prediction extracts time-varying features that depend on increasingly high-level statistics of the sensory input.
source: When applied hierarchically, temporal prediction extracts time-varying features that depend on increasingly high-level statistics of the sensory input.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model's behavior as demonstrated in the study.

claim: Temporal prediction would be useful for guiding future action, uncovering underlying variables, and discarding irrelevant information.
source: This would be useful for guiding future action, uncovering underlying variables, and discarding irrelevant information (Bialek et al., 2001; Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Temporal prediction relates to a class of principles including the predictive information bottleneck and slow feature analysis.
source: Temporal prediction relates to a class of principles, such as the predictive information bottleneck (Bialek et al., 2001; Chalk et al., 2018; Salisbury and Palmer, 2016) and slow feature analysis (Berkes and Wiskott, 2005), that similarly involve selectively encoding only features that are efficiently predictive of the future.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to related theoretical frameworks.

claim: Efficient coding, sparse coding, and predictive coding aim to efficiently represent all current and perhaps past input.
source: This class of principles has been contrasted (Chalk et al., 2018; Salisbury and Palmer, 2016) with other principles that are more typically used to explain sensory coding – efficient coding (Barlow, 1961; Bell and Sejnowski, 1997), sparse coding (Olshausen and Field, 1996), and predictive coding (Huang and Rao, 2011; Rao and Ballard, 1999) – that aim instead to efficiently represent all current and perhaps past input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on these coding principles.

claim: No single principle has so far been able to explain the diverse spatiotemporal tuning involved in motion processing that emerges along the visual stream, from retina to V1 to the extrastriate middle temporal area (MT).
source: Although these principles have been successful in accounting for various visual receptive field (RF) properties in V1 (Bell and Sejnowski, 1997; Berkes and Wiskott, 2005; Chalk et al., 2018; Olshausen and Field, 1996; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Singer et al., 2018), no single principle has so far been able to explain the diverse spatiotemporal tuning involved in motion processing that emerges along the visual stream, from retina to V1 to the extrastriate middle temporal area (MT).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Deep supervised network models optimized for image classification can reproduce some features of the visual system.
source: Some features of the visual system have been reproduced by deep supervised network models optimized for image classification using large labeled datasets (e.g. images labeled as cat, dog, car; Yamins and DiCarlo, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on supervised models.

claim: Supervised models can help explain the RF properties of the likely hard-wired retina.
source: While these models can help to explain the RF properties of the likely hard-wired retina (Lindsey et al., 2019), they are less informative if neuronal tuning is influenced by experience, as in cortex, since most sensory input is unlabeled except for sporadic reinforcement signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Most sensory input is unlabeled except for sporadic reinforcement signals.
source: While these models can help to explain the RF properties of the likely hard-wired retina (Lindsey et al., 2019), they are less informative if neuronal tuning is influenced by experience, as in cortex, since most sensory input is unlabeled except for sporadic reinforcement signals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the nature of sensory input.

claim: The temporal prediction approach is unsupervised and inherently applies to the temporal domain.
source: The temporal prediction approach is unsupervised (i.e. it requires no labeled data), and inherently applies to the temporal domain.
evidence: This describes a key property of the temporal prediction model presented in the study.

claim: Several theoretical studies have proposed prediction of future input as a primary function of neural systems.
source: Several theoretical studies have proposed prediction of future input as a primary function of neural systems (Bialek et al., 2001; Hawkins and Blakeslee, 2004; O'Reilly et al., 2014; Softky, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Models incorporating temporal prediction that explicitly attempt to explain features of sensory representations from natural inputs have only very recently started to emerge.
source: However, models incorporating temporal prediction that explicitly attempt, with varying degrees of success, to explain features of sensory representations from natural inputs have only very recently started to emerge (Chalk et al., 2018; Lotter et al., 2020; Ocko et al., 2018; Palm, 2012; Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent work in the field.

claim: A simple non-hierarchical model instantiating temporal prediction can account for temporal aspects of V1 simple cell RFs.
source: We have previously shown that a simple non-hierarchical model instantiating temporal prediction can account for temporal aspects of V1 simple cell RFs (Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The hierarchical temporal prediction model consists of stacked feedforward single-hidden-layer convolutional neural networks.
source: We instantiated temporal prediction as a hierarchical model consisting of stacked feedforward single-hidden-layer convolutional neural networks (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the model used in the study, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The first stack was trained to predict the immediate future frame (40ms) of unfiltered natural video inputs from the previous 5 frames (200ms).
source: The first stack was trained using backpropagation to predict the immediate future frame (40ms) of unfiltered natural video inputs from the previous 5 frames (200ms).
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the first stack of the model.

claim: Each subsequent stack was trained to predict the future hidden-unit activity of the stack below it from the past activity in response to the natural video inputs.
source: Each subsequent stack was then trained to predict the future hidden-unit activity of the stack below it from the past activity in response to the natural video inputs.
evidence: This describes the training procedure for subsequent stacks of the model.

claim: L1 regularization was applied to the weights of each stack, akin to a constraint on neural 'wiring'.
source: L1 regularization was applied to the weights of each stack, akin to a constraint on neural 'wiring'.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the model training procedure.

claim: The video inputs consisted of animals moving in natural environments, filmed with panning, still and occasionally zooming cameras.
source: The video inputs consisted of animals moving in natural environments, filmed with panning, still and occasionally zooming cameras.
evidence: This describes the training data used for the model.

claim: The videos were not bandpass filtered in the manner of Olshausen and Field, 1997.
source: Unlike in Singer et al., 2018, we did not bandpass filter the videos in the manner of Olshausen and Field, 1997.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the current study compared to prior work.

claim: The four stacks respectively used 50, 100, 200, and 400 convolutional units.
source: The four stacks respectively used 50, 100, 200, and 400 convolutional units, each having a particular convolutional kernel.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the model.

claim: After training, the RFs of the units in the first stack showed spatially localized, center-surround tuning with a decaying temporal envelope, characteristic of retinal and lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) neurons.
source: After training, we first examined the input weights of the units in the first stack. Each hidden unit can be viewed as a linear non-linear (LN) model (Chichilnisky, 2001; Simoncelli et al., 2004), as commonly used to describe neuronal RFs. With L1 regularization slightly above the optimum for prediction, the RFs of the units showed spatially localized, center-surround tuning with a decaying temporal envelope, characteristic of retinal and lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) neurons (Barlow, 1953; Kuffler, 1953; Shapley and Perry, 1986).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data.

claim: The model units' RFs have either an excitatory (ON) or inhibitory (OFF) blob-like structure at the 0 ms time-step, often with a surround of opposing sign in the same or previous time-step.
source: The model units' RFs have either an excitatory (ON) or inhibitory (OFF) blob-like structure at the 0 ms time-step, often with a surround of opposing sign in the same or previous time-step (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: Both ON and OFF units can have either small RFs that do not change polarity over time or large RFs that switch polarity over time.
source: Both ON and OFF units can have either small RFs that do not change polarity over time (Figure 3a, units 1–4; Figure 3b, bottom left), or large RFs that switch polarity over time (Figure 3a, units 5–6; Figure 3b, top right).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: The model units resemble the four main cell types in the primate retina and LGN: the parvocellular pathway ON/OFF neurons and the more change-sensitive magnocellular pathway ON/OFF neurons.
source: This is reminiscent of the four main cell types in the primate retina and LGN: the parvocellular pathway ON/OFF neurons and the more change-sensitive magnocellular pathway ON/OFF neurons, respectively (Shapley and Perry, 1986).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results, supported by citation to neurophysiological data.

claim: Decreasing L1-regularization strength causes the model RFs to change from center-surround tuning to Gabor-like tuning.
source: Interestingly, simply decreasing L1-regularization strength causes the model RFs to change from center-surround tuning to Gabor-like tuning, resembling localized, oriented bars that shift over time (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 3c.

claim: The balance between a code that is optimal for prediction and one that prioritizes efficient wiring might underlie differences in the retina and LGN of different species.
source: It is possible that this balance, between a code that is optimal for prediction and one that prioritizes efficient wiring, might underlie differences in the retina and LGN of different species.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the model results.

claim: The retina of mice and rabbits contains many neurons with oriented and direction-tuned RFs, whereas cats and macaques mostly have center-surround RFs.
source: The retina of mice and rabbits contains many neurons with oriented and direction-tuned RFs, whereas cats and macaques mostly have center-surround RFs (Scholl et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior neurophysiological work.

claim: Many of the resulting RFs in the second stack were Gabor-like over space, resembling those of V1 simple cells.
source: Using the trained center-surround-tuned network as the first stack, a second stack was added to the model and trained. The output of each second stack unit results from a linear-nonlinear-linear-nonlinear transformation of the visual input, and hence we estimated their RFs by reverse correlation with binary noise input. Many of the resulting RFs were Gabor-like over space (Figure 4a and b, I-II), resembling those of V1 simple cells (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: The RF envelopes in the second stack decayed into the past, and often showed spatial shifts or polarity changes over time, indicating direction or flicker sensitivity.
source: The RF envelopes decayed into the past, and often showed spatial shifts or polarity changes over time, indicating direction or flicker sensitivity, as is also seen in V1 (DeAngelis et al., 1993; Figure 4a and b, I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data.

claim: Most units in the second stack were selective for stimulus orientation, spatial and temporal frequency.
source: Using full-field drifting sinusoidal gratings (Figure 4a and b, III-IV), we found that most units were selective for stimulus orientation, spatial and temporal frequency (Figure 4a and b, V-VII), and some were also direction selective (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Responses to the optimal grating typically oscillate over time between a maximum when the grating is in phase with the RF and 0 when the grating is out of phase.
source: Responses to the optimal grating typically oscillate over time between a maximum when the grating is in phase with the RF and 0 when the grating is out of phase (Figure 4a and b, IV).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: These response characteristics are typical of V1 simple cells.
source: These response characteristics are typical of V1 simple cells (Movshon et al., 1978a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior neurophysiological work.

claim: Most units in the third and fourth stack are tuned for orientation, spatial frequency, temporal frequency and in some cases for direction.
source: In the third and fourth stack, we followed the same procedures as in the second stack. Most of these units are also tuned for orientation, spatial frequency, temporal frequency and in some cases for direction (Figure 5a and b, V-VII; Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: While some units in the third and fourth stack resembled simple cells, most resembled the complex cells of V1 and extrastriate visual areas.
source: However, while some units resembled simple cells, most resembled the complex cells of V1 and extrastriate visual areas (such as V2/V3/V4/MT; Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; Hu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data.

claim: Complex cells are tuned for orientation and spatial and temporal frequency, but are relatively invariant to the phase of the optimal grating.
source: Complex cells are tuned for orientation and spatial and temporal frequency, but are relatively invariant to the phase of the optimal grating Movshon et al., 1978b; each cell's response to its optimal grating has a high mean value and changes little with the grating's phase (Figure 5a and b, III-IV).
evidence: This describes a known property of complex cells, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: Whether a neuron is assigned as simple or complex is typically based on the modulation ratio in such plots (<1 indicates complex).
source: Whether a neuron is assigned as simple or complex is typically based on the modulation ratio in such plots (<1 indicates complex; Skottun et al., 1991).
evidence: This describes a standard method in neuroscience, supported by citation.

claim: Model units with low modulation ratios had little discernible structure in their RFs, another characteristic feature of V1 complex cells.
source: Model units with low modulation ratios had little discernible structure in their RFs (Figure 5a and b, I-II), another characteristic feature of V1 complex cells (Rust et al., 2005; Schwartz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data.

claim: The distribution of modulation ratios is bimodal in both macaque monkey V1 and the model.
source: The distribution of modulation ratios is bimodal in both macaque monkey V1 (Ringach et al., 2002; Skottun et al., 1991) and our model (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data and illustrated in Figure 6a.

claim: Both model and real neurons were typically orientation selective, but with the model units having weaker tuning as measured by orientation bandwidth.
source: Both model and real neurons were typically orientation selective, but with the model units having weaker tuning as measured by orientation bandwidth (median data [Ringach et al., 2002]: 23.5°, model: 37.5°; Figure 6b) and circular variance (median data [Ringach et al., 2002]: simple cells 0.45, complex cells 0.66; median model: simple cells 0.47, complex cells 0.85; Figure 6c and d).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Orientation-tuned units and direction-tuned units in the second stack were mostly simple, whereas those in subsequent stacks became increasingly complex.
source: Orientation-tuned units (circular variance <0.9 or orientation bandwidth <150°) and direction-tuned units (direction selectivity >0.1) in the second stack were mostly simple (modulation ratios >1), whereas those in subsequent stacks became increasingly complex (Figure 6a and c–f).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Circular variance varied with the modulation ratio in a similar way in both model and recorded V1 data.
source: Circular variance varied with the modulation ratio in a similar way in both model (Figures 6c–e) and recorded V1 data (Figure 6c–d and h).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to neurophysiological data and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Simple cell-like units tended to be more direction tuned than complex cell-like units.
source: Simple cell-like units (60% with DSI1 ≥0.5; n=95; Figure 6g) tended to be more direction tuned than complex cell-like units (19% with DSI1 ≥0.5, n=205; Figure 6g), as is seen in cat V1 (Kim and Freeman, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, supported by comparison to cited neurophysiological data and illustrated in Figure 6g.

claim: A clear progression from non-orientation-selective, to simple-cell-like, to complex-cell-like is seen in the units as one progresses up the stacks of the model.
source: A clear progression from non-orientation-selective, to simple-cell-like, to complex-cell-like is seen in the units as one progresses up the stacks of the model (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: This progression bears some resemblance to the progression from the retina and LGN to the geniculorecipient granular layer of V1 to the superficial layers of V1.
source: This bears some resemblance to the progression from the retina and LGN, which has few orientation-selective neurons, at least in cats and monkeys (Barlow, 1953; Kuffler, 1953; Shapley and Perry, 1986), to the geniculorecipient granular layer of V1, which tends to contain more simple cells, to the superficial layers of V1, where more complex cells have been found (Ringach et al., 2002; Cloherty and Ibbotson, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results, supported by citations to neurophysiological data.

claim: There is a substantial increase in the proportion of complex cells from V1 to extrastriate visual areas, such as V2.
source: This is also consistent with the substantial increase in the proportion of complex cells from V1 to extrastriate visual areas, such as V2 (Cloherty and Ibbotson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior neurophysiological work.

claim: Pattern-selective neurons solve the aperture problem by integrating over input from many direction-selective V1 complex cells.
source: Pattern-selective neurons solve this problem, likely by integrating over input from many direction-selective V1 complex cells (Movshon et al., 1985; Movshon and Newsome, 1996; Rust et al., 2006; Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998; Zeki, 1974), and hence respond selectively to the motion of patterns as a whole.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neurophysiological and theoretical work.

claim: Pattern-selective neurons have been found in macaque extrastriate cortical area MT, cat anterior ectosylvian visual area (AEV), ferret posterior suprasylvian sulcus (PSS), and even in mouse V1.
source: These neurons have been found in macaque extrastriate cortical area MT (Movshon et al., 1985; Rodman and Albright, 1989; Rust et al., 2006), cat anterior ectosylvian visual area (AEV) (Scannell et al., 1996), ferret posterior suprasylvian sulcus (PSS) (Lempel and Nielsen, 2019), and even in mouse V1 (Palagina et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neurophysiological work.

claim: Component-selective cells respond maximally when the plaid is oriented such that either one of its component gratings moves in the preferred direction of the cell.
source: In V1 and MT, component-selective cells respond maximally when the plaid is oriented such that either one of its component gratings moves in the preferred direction of the cell (as measured by a drifting grating). This results in two peaks in plaid-direction tuning curves (Movshon et al., 1985; Rust et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a known property of component-selective cells, supported by citations.

claim: Pattern-selective cells have a single peak in their direction tuning curves, when the plaid's direction of movement aligns with the preferred direction of the cell.
source: Conversely, pattern-selective cells have a single peak in their direction tuning curves, when the plaid's direction of movement aligns with the preferred direction of the cell (Movshon et al., 1985; Rust et al., 2006; Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a known property of pattern-selective cells, supported by citations.

claim: The model produces examples of both component-selective units (in stacks 2–4) and pattern-selective units (only in stack 4).
source: We see examples of both component-selective units (in stacks 2–4) and pattern-selective units (only in stack 4) in our model, as indicated by plaid-direction tuning curves (Figure 8b) and plots of response as a function of the directions of each component (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is a finding from the model, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Only 8% of the direction-selective units in stack 4 are pattern-motion selective.
source: Only a few (8%, n=3/37) of the direction-selective units in stack 4 are pattern-motion selective.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model.

claim: In MT, approximately 23% of neurons are pattern-motion selective.
source: This is a lower proportion than is seen in MT (~23%, n=179/792 [Wang and Movshon, 2016]), where the vast majority (>90%, [Wang and Movshon, 2016]) of neurons are direction sensitive (DSI >0.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior neurophysiological work.

claim: When the temporal prediction model was trained on videos with additional panning motion, there was a substantial increase in the proportion of direction-selective units in all stacks.
source: When we trained the temporal prediction model on this augmented dataset, we observed a substantial increase in the proportion of direction-selective units in all stacks, as well as an increase in the number of pattern-motion-selective units to 19, with some of them emerging in stacks 2 and 3 as well as stack 4.
evidence: This is a finding from the model when trained on augmented data.

claim: The hierarchical temporal prediction model is the first normative model that produces pattern-motion selectivity.
source: While there are phenomenological models (i.e. that are fitted to neural data) of pattern selectivity (Rust et al., 2006; Simoncelli and Heeger, 1998), to our knowledge, our model is the first normative model (i.e. where properties emerge from first principles applied to natural statistics) that produces this phenomenon.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model, supported by comparison to prior work.

claim: At least some hierarchy or recurrency in model structure is required to obtain complex-cell-like units.
source: At least some hierarchy or recurrency in model structure is required to obtain complex-cell-like units - the simple linear-nonlinear structure of hidden units in our previous non-hierarchical temporal prediction model is incapable of producing units resembling complex cells, although it can produce simple-cell-like units (Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison to prior work by the authors.

claim: A control model trained to efficiently estimate the present input given present and past input could not produce units resembling simple cells or complex cells.
source: When we trained this model with the same form and dataset as the temporal prediction model, we indeed found that while the first stack could reproduce the center-surround spatial tuning seen in the retina, the model unit RFs had no temporal structure – they only depended on the present time step. Furthermore, this control model could not produce magnocellular-like units that switch polarity, nor could it produce units at any stack that resembled simple cells or complex cells by inspection, either spatially or temporally (Figure 6—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a finding from a control model, illustrated in supplementary figures.

claim: Both hierarchy and temporal prediction acting together produce the diverse tuning properties observed in the model.
source: This suggests that both hierarchy and temporal prediction acting together produce the diverse tuning properties we observe in our model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control model results.

claim: A control model with shuffled input weights lacked discernable structure in RFs and could not produce center-surround, simple cells, complex cells or pattern-motion-selective cells.
source: As a further control model, we shuffled the input weights across space and time for each stack of the trained hierarchical temporal prediction model, and then probed the network with stimuli. In this case, the RFs in all stacks lacked discernable structure (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), and could not be fitted by Gabor functions, being neither center-surround nor simple-cell-like (only ~1% relative to the standard model met the criteria for simple-cell-like). To look for complex-cell-like units, we measured the model units' responses to drifting gratings (Figure 6—figure supplement 6). They showed only patchy selectivity for spatial and temporal frequency and orientation, and there were almost no (<1% relative to standard model) units responding like complex cells in any stack. In addition, none of the units showed pattern-motion-selectivity.
evidence: This is a finding from a control model, illustrated in supplementary figures.

claim: The precise ordering of the weights learned through temporal prediction is important for capturing the tuning phenomena observed in the brain.
source: The fact that we do not see center-surround, simple cells, complex cells or pattern-motion-selective cells shows that the precise ordering of the weights learned through temporal prediction (as opposed to these weights being randomly shuffled) is important for capturing the tuning phenomena observed in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control model results.

claim: When trained on videos with shuffled frame order, the model produced much fewer simple-cell-like and complex-cell-like units.
source: Finally, we examined the importance of temporal structure in the stimuli for the results seen in the model. To test this, we shuffled the order of the frames in each clip, reducing their similarity over time. In the first stack, center-surround spatial tuning remained, but temporal structure of the RFs spanned the full five frames available and without temporal asymmetry or increased weighting near the present. By inspection, no RFs resembled simple cells, and by our definitions, simple-cell-like units and complex-cell-like units were much rarer across stacks (~4% and~13% relative to the standard model). None of the units showed pattern-motion-selectivity.
evidence: This is a finding from a control model with shuffled temporal structure.

claim: The temporal prediction model rivals a supervised model (VGG) trained using a labeled behavioral dataset in predicting neural responses in V1 to dynamic stimuli.
source: Hence, the temporal prediction model, an unsupervised model trained on unlabeled data with no explicit constraints imposed by either neural or behavioral data, rivals a supervised model (VGG) trained using a labeled behavioral dataset in predicting neural responses in V1 to dynamic stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural response prediction analysis.

claim: For dynamic visual stimuli, the BWT, PredNet, autoencoder, and slowness models all performed worse than the temporal prediction model.
source: However, for the dynamic visual stimuli, the results were quite different (Figure 9B). The BWT, PredNet, autoencoder, and slowness models all performed worse than the temporal prediction model (bootstrap, n = 23, p = 1.6 × 10–2, p = 2 × 10–4, p = 2.5 × 10–3 and p <10–4, respectively), with only the VGG model being not significantly different (bootstrap, n = 23, n.s.).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the neural response prediction analysis, illustrated in Figure 9B.

claim: The temporal prediction model is a reasonable contender as an unsupervised model of V1 responses to natural stimuli, particularly dynamic natural stimuli.
source: Thus, the temporal prediction model is a reasonable contender as an unsupervised model of V1 responses to natural stimuli, particularly dynamic natural stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural response prediction analysis.

claim: The hierarchical temporal prediction model accounts for many spatial and temporal tuning properties of cells in the dorsal visual pathway, from the center-surround tuning of cells in the retina and LGN, to the spatiotemporal tuning and direction selectivity of V1 simple and complex cells, and to some degree the motion processing of pattern-selective cells.
source: This simple model accounts for many spatial and temporal tuning properties of cells in the dorsal visual pathway, from the center-surround tuning of cells in the retina and LGN, to the spatiotemporal tuning and direction selectivity of V1 simple and complex cells, and to some degree the motion processing of pattern-selective cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The hierarchical temporal prediction model can predict neural responses in V1 to movies of natural scenes to a level equal to or better than other models of visual processing.
source: Furthermore, it can predict neural responses in V1 to movies of natural scenes to a level equal to or better than other models of visual processing, such as supervised image recognition models, predictive coding models, and hierarchical sparse or slow activity models.
evidence: This is a summary of the neural response prediction findings.

claim: Whether the features are hard-wired by evolution or learned over the course of development likely depends on the region in question, with retina more hard-wired and cortex a mixture of innate tuning and learning from sensory input.
source: Although this work suggests that temporal prediction may explain why many features of sensory neurons take the form that they do, we are agnostic as to whether the features are hard-wired by evolution or learned over the course of development. This is likely to depend on the region in question, with retina more hard-wired and cortex a mixture of innate tuning and learning from sensory input (Huberman et al., 2008; Kiorpes, 2015).
evidence: This is a discussion point supported by citations to prior work.

claim: If the predictive features are learned, this suggests that while some neurons represent these features, a fraction of neurons in the cortex might represent the prediction error used to train the network.
source: If the predictive features are learned, this suggests that while some neurons represent these features, a fraction of neurons in the cortex (or elsewhere) might represent the prediction error used to train the network.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the biological implementation of the model.

claim: There is evidence that some cortical neurons may represent prediction error.
source: Indeed, there is evidence that some cortical neurons may represent prediction error (Auksztulewicz et al., 2023; Fiser et al., 2016; Rubin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neurophysiological work.

claim: The model does not require backpropagation across more than one hidden layer and isolates learning within each stack, reducing the need to find biologically plausible alternatives to backpropagation that scale with depth.
source: One advantage of our model, for comparison to the biology, is that it does not require backpropagation across more than one hidden layer and isolates learning within each stack, reducing the need to find biologically plausible alternatives to backpropagation that scale with depth (Bartunov et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an advantage of the model architecture for biological plausibility.

claim: Incorporating recurrent processing may lead to an improvement in the match between the number of pattern-selective units in the model and the proportion of these units seen in MT.
source: Incorporating recurrent processing may lead to an improvement in the match between the number of pattern-selective units in the model and the proportion of these units seen in MT, as this has been argued to be important by some (Pack et al., 2001), but not all (Rust et al., 2006) physiological studies of pattern-selectivity in MT.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future model development, supported by citations.

claim: Incorporating other types of motion into the training videos, such as self-motion or eye movements, may produce a closer match between the response properties of the model units and those seen in the biology.
source: Furthermore, the videos used to train our model typically involve animals moving in natural environments filmed with still or slowly panning cameras. Incorporating other types of motion into the training videos, such as self-motion or eye movements, may also produce a closer match between the response properties of our model units and those seen in the biology.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future model development.

claim: When additional panning was incorporated into the training videos, the proportion of pattern-motion-selective units in the model increased, providing an experimentally testable prediction from the model.
source: Indeed, when additional panning was incorporated into the training videos, the proportion of pattern-motion-selective units in the model increased, providing an experimentally testable prediction from our model.
evidence: This is a finding from the model and a prediction for future experiments.

claim: Although temporal prediction is proposed as an important method for extracting potentially useful features of natural inputs, additional constraints are likely to further refine those features that are of direct relevance to specific behavioral goals.
source: Finally, although we propose that temporal prediction is an important method for extracting potentially useful features of natural inputs, additional constraints are likely to further refine those features that are of direct relevance to specific behavioral goals.
evidence: This is a speculative discussion point about the scope of the model.

claim: Algorithms involving prediction have a long history of use in engineering and signal processing.
source: Algorithms involving prediction have a long history of use in engineering and signal processing (de Jager, 1952; Kalman, 1960; Kalman and Bucy, 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in engineering.

claim: The model has potential applications as an unsupervised learning algorithm to initialize deep networks for supervised tasks.
source: Our model also has potential applications for such use, for example, as an unsupervised learning algorithm to initialize deep networks for supervised tasks.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for potential applications of the model.

claim: One prediction common to all unsupervised models is that neurons in sensory cortex should learn stimulus feature selectivity that is dependent on stimulus statistics even in the absence of reinforcement signals.
source: One prediction common to all unsupervised models, which distinguishes them from supervised and reinforcement models, is that neurons in sensory cortex should learn stimulus feature selectivity that is dependent on stimulus statistics even in the absence of reinforcement signals.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the nature of unsupervised models.

claim: Rearing cats with goggles that restrict the range of visible orientations influences the orientation tuning of V1 neurons.
source: Some studies have shown that altering stimulus statistics can change cortical representations; for example, rearing cats with goggles that restrict the range of visible orientations influences the orientation tuning of V1 neurons (Tanaka et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Predictive coding suggests that the majority of feedforward projections between cortical regions should transmit prediction error, whereas temporal prediction suggests that these projections should transmit the presence of predictive features.
source: First, predictive coding suggests that the majority of feedforward projections between cortical regions should transmit prediction error, whereas temporal prediction suggests that these projections should transmit the presence of predictive features.
evidence: This is a prediction that distinguishes temporal prediction from predictive coding.

claim: Feedback connectivity is integral to perception in predictive coding, but not for temporal prediction.
source: Second, feedback connectivity is integral to perception in predictive coding, but not for temporal prediction.
evidence: This is a prediction that distinguishes temporal prediction from predictive coding.

claim: Many aspects of visual perception can occur so rapidly that there may not be time for feedback to operate.
source: Indeed, many aspects of visual perception can occur so rapidly that there may not be time for feedback to operate (Fabre-Thorpe, 2011; Thorpe et al., 1996), supportive of predominantly feed-forward models such as the one we present here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on rapid visual perception.

claim: Feedback connections may be important for contextually modulating neuronal selectivity, perhaps using higher level statistics to help predict lower level statistics.
source: This does, however, raise the question of what role feedback connections would play in the temporal prediction framework. We would suggest that they may be important for contextually modulating neuronal selectivity (Crist et al., 2001; Gilbert et al., 2001), perhaps using higher level statistics to help predict lower level statistics.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about the role of feedback, supported by citations.

claim: Temporal correlational structure in sensory input is extremely important for the temporal prediction model, but not for predictive coding, which can learn from still images.
source: Third, temporal correlational structure in sensory input is extremely important for the temporal prediction model, but not for predictive coding, which can learn from still images.
evidence: This is a prediction that distinguishes temporal prediction from predictive coding.

claim: An animal reared in a visual environment where the frame order of natural visual inputs is randomly shuffled should develop altered cortical tuning, not just in the temporal domain, but also in the spatial domain.
source: This implies that an animal reared in a visual environment, perhaps a virtual environment using goggles, where the frame order of natural visual inputs is randomly shuffled, should develop altered cortical tuning, not just in the temporal domain, but also in the spatial domain.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the temporal prediction model.

claim: A recent study reported that rearing rats in a box with frame-scrambled natural movies led to a substantial degradation and reduction in complex cells, consistent with the importance of temporal prediction.
source: A recent study (Matteucci and Zoccolan, 2020) reported that rearing rats in a box with frame-scrambled natural movies played upon the walls led to a substantial degradation and reduction in complex cells, consistent with the importance of temporal prediction, at least for those cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent experimental study.

claim: Sparse coding and ICA are the standard normative models of V1 simple cell RFs.
source: Among local models, sparse coding and ICA are the standard normative models of V1 simple cell RFs (Bell and Sejnowski, 1997; Olshausen, 2002; Olshausen and Field, 1997; Olshausen and Field, 1996; van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998; van Hateren and van der Schaaf, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on these models.

claim: Sparse coding and ICA models trained on static images are unable to account for the temporal aspects of neuronal RFs, such as direction selectivity or two-dimensional motion processing.
source: Typically, these models are trained using still natural images and have had remarkable success in accounting for the spatial features of V1 simple cell RFs (Bell and Sejnowski, 1997; Olshausen and Field, 1997; Olshausen and Field, 1996; van Hateren and van der Schaaf, 1998). However, models trained on static images are unable to account for the temporal aspects of neuronal RFs, such as direction selectivity or two-dimensional motion processing.
evidence: This is a limitation of prior models, supported by citations.

claim: ICA and sparse coding models extended to spatiotemporal inputs tend to produce symmetric temporal envelopes that do not match the asymmetric envelopes of real neurons.
source: The ICA and sparse coding frameworks have been extended to model features of spatiotemporal inputs (Chalk et al., 2018; Olshausen, 2002; van Hateren and Ruderman, 1998). While these models capture many of the spatial tuning properties of simple cells, they tend to produce symmetric temporal envelopes that do not match the asymmetric envelopes of real neurons (Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a limitation of prior models, supported by citations.

claim: SFA models find features with tuning properties that closely resemble those of V1 complex cells, including phase invariance to drifting sinusoidal gratings and end- and side-inhibition.
source: When trained to find slowly varying features in natural video inputs, SFA models (Berkes and Wiskott, 2005) find features with tuning properties that closely resemble those of V1 complex cells, including phase invariance to drifting sinusoidal gratings and end- and side-inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on SFA models.

claim: A sparse prior must be applied to the activities of the model units in SFA in order to produce spatial localization.
source: A sparse prior must be applied to the activities of the model units in order to produce spatial localization – a key feature of V1 complex cells (Lies et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on SFA models.

claim: SFA on its own does not provide a normative explanation for simple cells.
source: Although SFA can account for complex cell tuning, on its own this framework does not provide a normative explanation for simple cells.
evidence: This is a limitation of the SFA framework.

claim: Predictive coding has been used to explain some nonlinear tuning properties of neurons in V1, such as end-stopping.
source: When applied to natural images, predictive coding has been used to explain some nonlinear tuning properties of neurons in V1, such as end-stopping (Rao and Ballard, 1999), and, when constrained to have sparse responses, reproduces orientation tuning that resembles the spatial tuning of simple cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on predictive coding.

claim: It is not clear whether predictive coding can reproduce the phase-invariant tuning of complex cells, nor has it been shown to account for direction selectivity or pattern-motion sensitivity.
source: However, it is not clear whether this framework can reproduce the phase-invariant tuning of complex cells, nor has it been shown to account for direction selectivity or pattern-motion sensitivity (Movshon et al., 1985).
evidence: This is a limitation of predictive coding models.

claim: Hierarchical ICA models have been shown to produce simple-cell-like subunits in the first layer and phase-invariant tuning reminiscent of complex cells in the second layer.
source: Hierarchical ICA models (and related models) provide another approach. These consist of two-layer networks that are trained on natural images with an independence prior placed on the unit activities (Hyvärinen and Hoyer, 2000; Hyvärinen and Hoyer, 2001; Karklin and Lewicki, 2009; Osindero et al., 2006). They have been shown to produce simple-cell-like subunits in the first layer of the network and phase-invariant tuning reminiscent of complex cells in the second layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on hierarchical ICA models.

claim: Hierarchical ICA models typically incorporate aspects that specifically encourage complex cell-like characteristics in the form of a quadratic nonlinearity resembling the complex cell energy model.
source: However, these models typically incorporate aspects that specifically encourage complex cell-like characteristics in the form of a quadratic nonlinearity resembling the complex cell energy model (Adelson and Bergen, 1985).
evidence: This describes a limitation of hierarchical ICA models, supported by citation.

claim: In some hierarchical ICA models, phase invariance is enforced by requiring the outputs of individual subunits to be uncorrelated.
source: In some models, phase invariance is enforced by requiring the outputs of individual subunits to be uncorrelated (Hyvärinen and Hoyer, 2000; Körding et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on hierarchical ICA models.

claim: In the temporal prediction model, phase invariance is learned as a consequence of the general principle of finding features that can efficiently predict future input.
source: This is in contrast to our model where the phase invariance is learned as a consequence of the general principle of finding features that can efficiently predict future input.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the temporal prediction model over hierarchical ICA models.

claim: An advantage to learning the invariance is that the identical model architecture can then be applied hierarchically to explain features in higher visual areas without changing the form of the model.
source: An advantage to learning the invariance is that the identical model architecture can then be applied hierarchically to explain features in higher visual areas without changing the form of the model.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the temporal prediction model.

claim: Hierarchical models based on temporal coherence have been shown to capture properties of both simple and complex cells.
source: Some hierarchical models based on temporal coherence have been trained on spatiotemporal inputs (videos of natural scenes). These models have been shown to capture properties of both simple and complex cells (Hurri and Hyvärinen, 2003; Kayser et al., 2001; Körding et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on temporal coherence models.

claim: Models that combine sparsity/independence priors with a temporal slowness constraint produce units with both simple and complex cell selectivity.
source: Other models have combined sparsity/independence priors with a temporal slowness constraint in a hierarchical model (Berkes et al., 2009; Cadieu and Olshausen, 2012; Chen et al., 2018; Hyvärinen et al., 2003). Since sparsity constraints tend to produce simple cell tuning and slowness constraints result in complex cell tuning, these models produce units with both types of selectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on combined models.

claim: The temporal prediction model produces both simple and complex cell selectivity with a single objective.
source: This contrasts with our model, which produces both types of selectivity with a single objective and also accounts for some tuning features of higher visual areas.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the temporal prediction model over combined models.

claim: PredNet captures some interesting physiological or psychophysical aspects of visual processing, such as end-stopping, sequence learning, illusory contours and the flash-lag effect.
source: PredNet captures some interesting physiological or psychophysical aspects of visual processing, such as end-stopping, sequence learning, illusory contours and the flash-lag effect (Lotter et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on PredNet.

claim: It has not been demonstrated that PredNet captures the parvocellular/magnocellular division, orientation- and direction-tuned simple and complex cells, and pattern-direction selectivity.
source: However, it has not been demonstrated that PredNet captures the phenomena that we describe, namely the parvocellular/magnocellular division, orientation- and direction-tuned simple and complex cells, and pattern-direction selectivity.
evidence: This describes a limitation of PredNet compared to the temporal prediction model.

claim: It can be difficult to determine whether the success or failure of a given model to predict neural responses is a consequence of the key principles underlying the model or the details of its implementation.
source: It is important to note that it can be difficult to determine whether the success or failure of a given model to predict neural responses is a consequence of the key principles underlying the model or the details of its implementation.
evidence: This is a caveat about interpreting model comparisons.

claim: The analysis should not be seen as definitively ruling out the principles underlying any of the other models, but rather an attempt to ascertain whether temporal prediction is a good contender for an underlying principle.
source: Thus, our analysis should not be seen as definitively ruling out the principles underlying any of the other models, but rather an attempt to ascertain whether temporal prediction is a good contender for an underlying principle.
evidence: This is a caveat about the scope of the model comparison.

claim: The VGG model is a supervised model fitted to human behavioral data (labeled images), whereas the other models are unsupervised normative models.
source: It is also important to point out that while the sparsity, slowness and PredNet models are, like temporal prediction, unsupervised normative models, the wavelet model is a descriptive model, and the VGG model is a supervised model fitted to human behavioral data (labeled images).
evidence: This describes a key difference between the models being compared.

claim: The VGG model is in some senses a fitted descriptive encoding model, rather than a normative unsupervised model.
source: Thus, in some senses, the VGG model is a fitted descriptive encoding model, rather than a normative unsupervised model.
evidence: This describes a key difference between VGG and the temporal prediction model.

claim: The performance of the hierarchical temporal prediction model at predicting the responses of V1 neurons to images was not substantially different from that of leading models, such as the VGG model.
source: We found that the performance of the hierarchical temporal prediction model at predicting the responses of V1 neurons to images was not substantially different from that of leading models, such as the VGG model.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural response prediction analysis.

claim: For the V1 responses to movies, the temporal prediction model outperformed all the other models, except for the VGG model which it performed as well as.
source: Importantly, for the V1 responses to movies, the temporal prediction model outperformed all the other models, except for the VGG model which it performed as well as.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural response prediction analysis.

claim: The VGG model has the advantage of labeled data, and was also trained on far more data than the temporal prediction model.
source: However, the VGG model has the advantage of labeled data, and was also trained on far more data than our model, whereas the temporal prediction model is unsupervised.
evidence: This describes a key difference in the training of the models.

claim: The findings indicate that temporal prediction remains a leading contender as an underlying normative unsupervised principle governing the neural processing of natural visual scenes.
source: Our findings therefore indicate that temporal prediction remains a leading contender as an underlying normative unsupervised principle governing the neural processing of natural visual scenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural response prediction analysis.

claim: Previous studies using principles related to temporal prediction have produced non-hierarchical models of the retina or primary sensory cortex.
source: Previous studies using principles related to temporal prediction have produced non-hierarchical models of the retina or primary sensory cortex and demonstrated retina-like RFs (Ocko et al., 2018), simple-cell like RFs (Chalk et al., 2018; Singer et al., 2018), or RFs resembling those found in primary auditory cortex (Singer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Any general principle of neural representation should be extendable to a hierarchical form and not tailored to the region it is attempting to explain.
source: However, any general principle of neural representation should be extendable to a hierarchical form and not tailored to the region it is attempting to explain.
evidence: This is a general principle about what constitutes a good model.

claim: Temporal prediction can be made hierarchical and reproduces the major motion-tuning properties that emerge along the visual pathway from retina and LGN to V1 granular layers to V1 superficial layers and potentially some properties of the extrastriate dorsal cortical pathway.
source: Here, we show that temporal prediction can indeed be made hierarchical and that it reproduces the major motion-tuning properties that emerge along the visual pathway from retina and LGN to V1 granular layers to V1 superficial layers and potentially some properties of the extrastriate dorsal cortical pathway.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The model captures not only linear tuning features, such as those seen in center-surround retinal neurons and direction-selective simple cells, but also nonlinear features seen in complex cells, with some indication that it may also reproduce properties of the pattern-sensitive neurons that are found in area MT.
source: This model captures not only linear tuning features, such as those seen in center-surround retinal neurons and direction-selective simple cells, but also nonlinear features seen in complex cells, with some indication that it may also reproduce properties of the pattern-sensitive neurons that are found in area MT.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: The capacity of the hierarchical temporal prediction model to account for many tuning features at several levels of the visual system suggests that the same framework may well explain many more features of the brain than have so far been investigated.
source: The capacity of our hierarchical temporal prediction model to account for many tuning features at several levels of the visual system suggests that the same framework may well explain many more features of the brain than we have so far investigated.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the broader applicability of the model.

claim: Iterated application of temporal prediction could be used to make predictions about the tuning properties of neurons in brain pathways that are much less well understood than those of the visual system.
source: Iterated application of temporal prediction, as performed by our model, could be used to make predictions about the tuning properties of neurons in brain pathways that are much less well understood than those of the visual system.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about future applications of the model.

claim: By learning behaviorally useful features from dynamic unlabeled data, temporal prediction may represent a fundamental coding principle in the brain.
source: Our results suggest that, by learning behaviorally useful features from dynamic unlabeled data, temporal prediction may represent a fundamental coding principle in the brain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
